pages.name: An empty capacitor
pages.task: An empty capacitor meets a 325 V peak through 1 Ω: what current flows at the first instant?

pages.name: Switching on at a zero
pages.text: Switched on at a zero with an empty core, the flux climbs to 2.0 times its normal peak. The current spikes red to 12 times full load.
pages.alt: A ring core with one winding and a switch to a 440 V supply. Beside it a flux bar and a B-H curve with its knee. Below, on one time axis, the supply voltage, the core flux and the primary current. Switched on 0° after a rising voltage zero, with an empty core. The flux overshoots the knee and the current spikes red.

pages.name: Flux left in
pages.task: Switched on at a zero with 0.6 left in, how high does the flux climb?

pages.name: At a peak
pages.text: Switched on at a peak with an empty core, the flux swings only to its normal peak. The current stays at 0.02 times full load.
pages.alt: A ring core with one winding and a switch to a 440 V supply. Beside it a flux bar and a B-H curve with its knee. Below, on one time axis, the supply voltage, the core flux and the primary current. Switched on 90° after a rising voltage zero, with an empty core. The flux stays below the knee and the current stays small.

pages.name: A trip on closing
pages.task: A breaker trips on closing onto a transformer, then holds. What most likely tripped it?
pages.why: The first close caught a worse moment on the wave, with flux left in the same way. Inrush can even look like an internal fault to differential protection.
pages.alt: A ring core with one winding and a switch to a 440 V supply. Beside it a flux bar and a B-H curve with its knee. Below, on one time axis, the supply voltage, the core flux and the primary current. Switched on 0° after a rising voltage zero, with 0.8 of the normal peak flux left in. The flux overshoots the knee and the current spikes red.
options: An overload on the 115 V side

pages.name: A current transformer
pages.text: A current transformer, a CT, is fed a current, not a voltage. Its primary is a busbar through its core, one turn carrying 400 A. The circuit's load sets that current. The 80-turn secondary drives 5 A round the meter. Its ampere-turns almost cancel the busbar's. The small difference makes the flux, just enough for the volts that push 5 A round. The meter circuit's resistance is the CT's [[burden]]. Its own winding has 0.2 Ω, so even shorted it needs 5 × 0.2 = 1.0 V.
pages.alt: A busbar carrying 400 A passes once through a ring core. Its 80-turn secondary feeds a meter circuit that is shorted. A flux bar beside it stays inside the knee. Below, two cycles of busbar current and secondary voltage: the voltage is a small wave in step with the current.

pages.name: Volts for 5 A
pages.task: 5 A through 0.2 Ω of winding and a 0.6 Ω meter circuit: what voltage must the secondary make?
pages.why: 5 × 0.8 = 4.0 V. That is 13% of the 30 V knee.
pages.alt: A busbar carrying 400 A passes once through a ring core. Its 80-turn secondary feeds a meter circuit that is 0.6 Ω. A flux bar beside it stays inside the knee. Below, two cycles of busbar current and secondary voltage: the voltage is a small wave in step with the current.

pages.name: An open secondary
pages.text: With the secondary open and 400 A in the busbar, the core saturates. The secondary spikes red at every flip.
pages.alt: A busbar carrying 400 A passes once through a ring core. Its 80-turn secondary feeds a meter circuit that is open. A flux bar beside it sits past the knee. Below, two cycles of busbar current and secondary voltage: the voltage sits flat with tall, narrow red spikes off the scale.

pages.name: Changing a meter
pages.task: A CT-fed ammeter must be changed with the circuit on load. What do you do first?
pages.answer: Short the CT's secondary at its shorting terminals
pages.why: The short keeps the ampere-turns balanced while the meter is out.
pages.alt: A busbar carrying 400 A passes once through a ring core. Its 80-turn secondary feeds a meter circuit that is shorted. A flux bar beside it stays inside the knee. Below, two cycles of busbar current and secondary voltage: the voltage is a small wave in step with the current.
options: Short the CT's secondary at its shorting terminals
Wait for a light load, then disconnect
Fit a fuse in the secondary

pages.name: No isolation
pages.text: An [[auto-transformer]] gives no isolation. It is one winding with a tap, so its output is joined to its input. An earth fault on either side is an earth fault on both. So it cannot make a separate insulated system. The supply's current is the power ÷ 440. It flows straight on into the load at 115 V, so it carries 115 ÷ 440 of the power, 26%. Only the other 74% is transformed and needs iron and copper. So an auto is much smaller only near a 1:1 ratio.

pages.name: Share transformed
pages.task: An auto-transformer steps 440 V to 400 V: what share of its power is transformed?
pages.why: 400 ÷ 440 = 0.909. Then 1 − 0.909 = 0.091, so 9%. Only that 9% needs iron and copper, so this auto can be much smaller than an isolating one.

pages.name: Shorting a VT
pages.task: What happens if a VT's secondary is shorted?
pages.why: Its voltage drives a large current through its own small impedance, like any power transformer's.
options: Nothing, as a CT runs shorted
It spikes, as an open CT does
